commands.short: Show the audit log: who did what, where, and the result
commands.long:
Every change komando makes, and every blocked attempt, is a sealed record in
~/.komando/store.db: when, who (and which AI agent), the command, its
targets and whether it worked. The newest entries come last.

--since and --until take how long ago (30m, 12h, 7d), today, yesterday,
or a time (2026-11-07, '2026-11-07 14:30', 2026-11-07T14:30:00Z); a time
without a zone is this computer's. --since keeps entries from that moment
on, --until those before it. With either, every match is shown unless -n
is given.
commands.example:
komando audit                      # the last 50
  komando audit -n 0 --target @prod  # everything about @prod
  komando audit --command host. --failed
  komando audit --since 2h           # everything in the last two hours
  komando audit --since yesterday --until today --target @prod
  komando audit --actor claude --since 7d        # what Claude Code did this week
  komando audit verify               # was the log changed outside komando?

flags.name: actor
flags.usage: only what this one did: part of the name in KOMANDO_ACTOR, the AI agent (claude, codex ...) or the computer account

flags.name: command
flags.usage: only commands that start with this (like exec, svc.)

flags.name: failed
flags.usage: only actions that failed or were blocked

flags.name: limit
flags.usage: the newest N entries (0 = all; with --since or --until, all unless given)

flags.name: since
flags.usage: only entries from this time on: 2h, 7d, today, 2026-11-07 or '2026-11-07 14:30'

flags.name: target
flags.usage: only entries for these servers or conns (a selector, like @prod)

flags.name: until
flags.usage: only entries before this time (the same forms as --since)

commands.short: Caches (Redis, Valkey, memcached): read and change keys
commands.long:
Read and change keys in Redis, Valkey or memcached. Add a cache with
`komando cache add`.

get, keys and info only read. set changes data (a protected cache asks
first); rm deletes keys, so it also needs --allow-dangerous. `cache run`
sends any command, but only reads unless --write; commands that flush,
block, run scripts or reconfigure the server also need --allow-dangerous.
commands.example:
komando cache add prod-redis redis://default@10.0.0.7:6379/0 --via web1 --ask-password
  komando cache info prod-redis
  komando cache keys prod-redis 'session:*'
  komando cache get prod-redis session:42
  komando cache set prod-redis maintenance on --ttl 30m --dry-run

commands.short: Check when the certificates of servers and websites expire
commands.long:
Reads certificates and says when they expire. It only reads.

A server (or @group, tag:, ...): komando looks for the certificates the
server uses: certbot's /etc/letsencrypt/live/*/cert.pem and the files that
nginx (ssl_certificate), haproxy (crt) and apache (SSLCertificateFile) name,
plus any --path. Files that need root are read with sudo only when sudo
works without a password; komando never asks for one. Only the CERTIFICATE
blocks of a file leave the server: a private key in the same file never
does. When certbot is there, the state of its renewal timer is shown too.

A website (https://example.com, example.com:443) or a conn that uses TLS:
komando connects from this computer (or through --via, or the conn's own
--via), reads the certificate the server sends and checks that it is
trusted and matches the name.

A certificate that expires within --warn (default 30d), has expired, is not
trusted, or a certbot renewal that failed is a problem: the command then
exits 1 (code CERT_PROBLEMS), like `komando doctor`.
commands.example:
komando cert check web1
  komando cert check @prod --warn 14d
  komando cert check https://shop.example.com api.example.com:8443
  komando cert check https://intranet.local --via bastion
  komando cert check web1 --path /etc/ssl/private/site.pem

flags.name: path
flags.usage: also check this certificate file (or folder) on the servers

flags.name: via
flags.usage: reach websites through this server or VPN (a --via path)

flags.name: warn
flags.usage: flag certificates that expire within this time (like 30d, 72h)

commands.short: Kubernetes and Docker Swarm: check, read logs, roll out, scale
commands.long:
TARGET is a Kubernetes cluster (bring yours in with `komando import
kubeconfig`) or a Swarm manager server. The same verbs work on both. Reads
need nothing; restart, scale and apply change the cluster (protected targets
need --yes; try --dry-run); rm needs --allow-dangerous. Anything else:
`cluster run` passes the native kubectl or docker command, read-only unless
--write.

A cluster's usual namespace is its kubeconfig context's; change it with
`komando conn edit NAME --option namespace=shop`, or name one per command
with --namespace.
commands.example:
komando import kubeconfig                       # one cluster per kubeconfig context
  komando cluster status prod-k8s                     # version, nodes, what is not healthy
  komando cluster list prod-k8s pods --namespace shop
  komando cluster logs prod-k8s deploy/api --namespace shop -f
  komando cluster deploy prod-k8s deploy/api --image ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.3 --namespace shop --wait

commands.short: Apply Kubernetes YAML or deploy a Swarm stack
commands.long:
Kubernetes: applies every object in FILE server-side and says per object
whether it was created, configured or unchanged. --dry-run asks the server
what would change and shows it as a diff (Secret values stay hidden; a
changed value shows as "[hidden, changed]"). Objects without a namespace go
to --namespace; one that names another namespace is refused.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

A field another field manager owns (an autoscaler's replicas, a kubectl
edit) stops the apply with K8S_CONFLICT naming that manager, and nothing
is applied. --force-conflicts takes those fields over, as
`kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts` does.

Swarm: deploys FILE (a compose file) as the stack --stack; --dry-run checks
the file with `docker stack config` on the manager.
commands.example:
komando cluster apply prod-k8s --file app.yaml --dry-run
  komando cluster apply prod-k8s --file app.yaml
  komando cluster apply swarm1 --file compose.yml --stack shop

write --image NAME=IMAGE). --wait stays until every replica runs the new
image, the rollout fails, or --timeout (default 5m) passes; go back with
`komando cluster rollback`.

conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

komando cluster deploy prod-k8s deployment/api --image ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.3 --namespace shop --wait
  komando cluster deploy prod-k8s deployment/api --image ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.3 --namespace shop --wait --dry-run
  komando cluster deploy swarm1 service/web --image nginx:1.27 --wait

commands.usage: komando cluster exec TARGET POD|TYPE/NAME -- COMMAND... [flags]
commands.short: Run a command in a pod, checked by the policy
commands.long:
Runs COMMAND in the pod (for TYPE/NAME, in one of its pods) and returns its
output. Commands that only look can say so with --read-only: it runs only
commands komando knows only read (cat, ls, printenv ...) and refuses any
other; a protected cluster then needs no --yes. For an
interactive shell use `komando cluster shell TARGET POD`.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when the command matches a
destructive rule: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to
go on, and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; on a protected
server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.
commands.example:
komando cluster exec prod-k8s deploy/api --namespace shop --read-only -- cat /app/config.yml
  komando cluster exec prod-k8s api-7d9f-x2 -c api --namespace shop -- php artisan cache:clear

Only this computer can use it. For a service, REMOTE is the service's port;
komando forwards to the pod's port behind it.

  komando cluster forward prod-k8s deploy/db 15432:5432 --namespace shop

commands.long:
Without --revision, a deployment goes back to the newest earlier revision
that runs other images than now. After a rollback, the revision it replaced
(the broken one) is skipped, so a second rollback does not bring it back;
--revision picks any revision. A Swarm service goes back to its previous
version.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

komando cluster rollback prod-k8s deployment/api --namespace shop --wait

  komando cluster rollback prod-k8s deployment/api --revision 3 --namespace shop
  komando cluster rollback swarm1 service/web

commands.short: Run any kubectl or docker command (read only by default)
commands.long:
For Kubernetes, komando runs the kubectl command itself (no kubectl
needed) and reaches the API through the conn's --via path: get (tables,
wide, name, json, yaml, jsonpath, custom-columns, -w), describe, logs,
events, top, explain, version, api-resources, api-versions, cluster-info,
auth can-i/whoami, wait, rollout, apply, diff, create, replace, delete,
patch, label, annotate, scale, set image, cordon, uncordon, drain, taint,
run, exec, cp, debug, certificate and config. For Swarm, docker runs on the
manager. Commands that change things need --write; delete, drain and other
risky verbs also need --allow-dangerous.

Settings:

  default_user     a login name
      user for servers that have none (empty: your own user name)
  default_timeout  duration > 0
      how long a remote command may run (--timeout overrides it)
  connect_timeout  duration > 0
      how long connecting may take (--connect-timeout overrides it)
  parallel         1 or more
      how many servers a command works on at once (-P overrides it)
  max_output_bytes 1024 or more
      output kept per stream and server, in bytes (--max-output overrides it)
  audit            on | off
      keep the audit log (turning it off needs --yes)
  audit_sql        full | hash | off
      how SQL text is kept in the audit log: hash keeps a SHA-256 so repeated queries can be matched (off needs --yes)

  mask_personal    protected | all | off

commands.short: Copy files, written SRC DST with TARGET:PATH (upload/download)
commands.long:
Remote paths are written TARGET:PATH (TARGET: alone, or TARGET:~/x, is the
login user's home folder). Uploads accept any target selector (@group,
tag:x, ...) and run in parallel. Downloads from several servers go to
DST/<server>/... . A single-file copy reports its sha256, so you can check
it. TARGET can be a storage conn too (backups:2026/db.sql.gz). cp is upload
or download written the cp way: the same code, flags and results.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

With TARGET:PATH on both sides, cp copies from one server or storage conn
to another (server to server, storage to storage, or one of each). The
data streams through this computer and is never saved on its disk. The
file at the destination is replaced, as an upload replaces it.

--continue goes on with a single file that was cut off: the part already
at the destination is kept when it matches the source (sha256), the rest
is sent, and the whole file is checked against the source. A destination
that is longer, or differs, stops with RESUME_CONFLICT and is not touched.
S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob and WebDAV store a file whole and
cannot add to one (RESUME_UNSUPPORTED).

Folders (-r), like cp and rsync:
  SRC/  (trailing slash)  the contents of SRC go into DST
  SRC   into a new DST    DST becomes the copy of SRC
  SRC   into a folder DST of the same name (site -> /var/www/site): DST is
        updated in place, so running the same copy again never nests site/site
  SRC   into another existing folder DST: the copy is DST/SRC
Symbolic links are not copied (they are listed as skipped). For repeatable
deploys that send only changed files, use `komando sync`.
commands.example:
komando cp ./app.tar.gz @web:/tmp/app.tar.gz
  komando cp -r ./site web1:/var/www/site
  komando cp ./nginx.conf web1:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf --sudo
  komando cp web1:/var/log/nginx/error.log ./logs/
  komando cp @web:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf ./configs/
  komando cp ./db.sql.gz backups:2026/db.sql.gz
  komando cp web1:/var/backups/db.sql.gz web2:/var/backups/
  komando cp -r web1:/var/www/site backups:sites/
  komando cp web1:/var/backups/db.sql.gz ./db.sql.gz --continue

commands.short: Save a copy of a database to a file on this computer
commands.long:
Saves a copy of the database to a file on this computer. Without --to the
file is CONN-<date>.sql.gz (SQLite: CONN-<date>.db) in this
folder. A file ending in .gz is compressed. Afterwards komando prints the
command that loads it back.

pg_dump or mysqldump runs on a server that has it: the one you name with
--run-on HOST, else the database's --via server. It connects to the conn
URL's address from that server, runs at low priority (nice, ionice) and
streams the backup back over SSH. Without such a server (a direct connection
or a VPN) komando writes plain SQL itself. PostgreSQL can also write its own
archive with --format custom (compressed, restored with pg_restore; needs
pg_dump on a server). --table and --schema-only narrow the dump. SQLite
databases are copied as a database file instead. An existing FILE is never
overwritten. The file holds your data: it is created readable only by you.
commands.example:
komando db dump prod-db                  # saves prod-db-<date>.sql.gz here
  komando db dump prod-db --to backups/    # the same name, inside backups/
  komando db dump prod-db --to prod-2026-11-02.sql.gz
  komando db dump prod-db --to prod.dump --format custom
  komando db dump prod-db --to prod.dump --format custom --run-on db1
  komando db dump prod-db --to orders.sql --table public.orders --table public.order_items
  komando db dump prod-db --to schema.sql --schema-only
  komando db dump local --to backup.db

commands.short: Stop a session's running query (--session ends the connection)
commands.long:
Find the PID with `komando db activity` or `komando db locks`. Without
--session only the running query stops (its transaction rolls back) and the
client stays connected. --dry-run shows the session it would stop. SQL
Server can only end a session (KILL), so there it needs --session. On Oracle
the PID is the SID that db activity shows. On ClickHouse it is the number db
activity shows for the query (made from its query_id); ClickHouse stops
queries, not connections, so there is no --session. On Snowflake, too, the
PID is the number db activity shows for the query; --session ends its
session (SYSTEM$ABORT_SESSION). On BigQuery it is the number db activity
shows for a job, which db kill cancels (jobs.cancel); there is no --session.
On MongoDB the PID is the opid that db activity shows; db kill stops that
operation (killOp) and the client stays connected, so there is no --session.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

  komando db kill prod-db 4821 --session --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes

commands.short: Run SQL (read only by default)
commands.long:
Runs SQL on a database and prints the rows. Without --write it only reads:
komando runs it in a read-only transaction, and stops it after 30s.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when the SQL deletes data
(DROP, DELETE without WHERE, ...): dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person
types the name to go on, and an AI agent or a script needs
--allow-dangerous; on a protected server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as
well.

More about db query:
A run stops after 30s unless --timeout (or the statement_timeout option in
the database URL) allows more. Placeholders take their values from
--arg, in order. -o csv and -o tsv print every row (up to --limit, if
given) for spreadsheets and scripts.
SQL that starts with a -- comment: pass it after -- or with -f -.

SQL Server has no read-only transaction: without --write komando rolls the
SQL back, and a statement it does not know as a read (a bare procedure
name, EXEC) needs --write. Its placeholders are @p1, @p2, ...

Oracle: placeholders are :1, :2, ... A PL/SQL block (BEGIN ... END;) runs
to the end of the text or to a line with only /, and needs --write and
--allow-dangerous. DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, GRANT) commits on its own in
Oracle, so it needs --write, goes on its own, and a dry run only reports it.

ClickHouse has no transactions: without --write every request carries the
server's own readonly=1, and a statement that is not a read (INSERT, ALTER,
CREATE, ...) needs --write, goes on its own, and a dry run only reports it.
Placeholders are {p1:String}, {p2:UInt64}, ... (named p1, p2, with a type).

Snowflake has no read-only mode komando can switch on, and each statement
is a session of its own: without --write komando sends only what it rates
as a read, and a statement that is not a read needs --write, goes on its
own, and a dry run only reports it. Log in with a role that may only
read. Placeholders are ?.

BigQuery: each statement first goes as a dry run, which runs nothing and
says what BigQuery sees and how many bytes it would read (which is what
BigQuery bills). Without --write only a SELECT runs. A query that would
read more than --max-bytes (default 10GB) does not run, and the job
carries that cap too. A write needs --write, goes on its own, and
--write --dry-run shows BigQuery's dry run. Placeholders are ?; the values
go as STRING, so write CAST(? AS INT64) for a number.

On MongoDB the text is a command document in JSON, its first key
naming it ({"find": ...}, {"aggregate": ...}, {"update": ...}). komando rates
it as it rates SQL: what it does not know as a read needs --write. "$db"
picks another database than the URL's.
commands.example:
komando db query prod-db "select id, email from users order by id desc limit 10"
  komando db query mongo-db '{"find": "users", "filter": {"plan": "pro"}, "limit": 10}'   # MongoDB
  komando db query prod-db "select * from users where email = $1" --arg bob@example.com
  komando db query prod-db --write --dry-run "update users set plan = 'pro' where id = 42"
  komando db query prod-db --file migration.sql --write --dry-run
  komando db query prod-db -o csv "select * from orders" > orders.csv
  komando db query bq "select count(*) from shop.orders" --max-bytes 50GB   # BigQuery

commands.short: Load a backup into a database
commands.long:
Runs the SQL in FILE (from `db dump`, pg_dump, mysqldump or any plain SQL
file; .gz is read compressed). komando runs the SQL itself, through the
conn's --via path, never with psql or mysql. A PostgreSQL archive (`db dump
--format custom`) is recognized by its content and loaded with pg_restore on
a server: the one named with --run-on HOST, else the database's --via
server; the archive is streamed to it over SSH.

Safety: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to go on,
and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; on a protected server
or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

In a terminal komando first offers to save a copy of the database as it is
now (db dump), so you can go back. Scripts and AI agents get no question:
run `komando db dump CONN` yourself first.

A restore can overwrite existing data, so it needs --allow-dangerous, plus
--yes on a protected database. The whole file is checked first: client
commands that could run programs (\! or system) and SQL komando cannot
follow (a file ending inside a quote, a change to how quotes are read) are
refused, and SQL that runs programs, touches server files or changes
privileges is named in the approval.

PostgreSQL restores run in one transaction: on any error nothing changes.
MySQL runs the statements in order and stops at the first error.
commands.example:
komando db restore staging-db --from prod-2026-11-02.sql.gz --dry-run   # checks the file, changes nothing
  komando db restore staging-db --from prod-2026-11-02.sql.gz --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes
  komando db restore staging-db --from prod.dump --run-on db1 --dry-run
  komando db restore staging-db --from prod.dump --run-on db1 --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes

commands.short: Download files from servers or from file storage
commands.long:
PATH is the path on the servers, or the key in the storage conn. --to is
where it lands: a file name, or a folder (existing, or ending in /); a
folder per server when several are picked. A file that is already here is
replaced only with --overwrite: without it, one file stops with FILE_EXISTS,
and a folder keeps them (kept) and copies the rest. --sudo reads one file
as root (up to 512 MiB).

--to - streams one file to stdout, from a server or storage: stdout has the
file's bytes and nothing else, whatever -o says, and komando's own answer
(the result with bytes and sha256, or the error) goes to stderr.

--continue goes on with a download of one file that was cut off: the part
already here is kept when it matches the source (sha256), the rest is
fetched, and the whole file is checked. A file here that is longer, or
differs, stops with RESUME_CONFLICT and is not touched.

Folders (-r), like cp and rsync:
  PATH/  (trailing slash)  the contents of PATH go into --to
  PATH   into a new --to    --to becomes the copy of PATH
  PATH   into a folder --to of the same name (/var/log/app -> ./app): it
         is updated in place, so downloading again never nests app/app
  PATH   into another existing folder --to: the copy is --to/NAME
Without --to it lands in the current folder under its own name. Symbolic
links are not copied (they are listed as skipped).
commands.example:
komando download web1 /var/log/nginx/error.log --to ./logs/
  komando download @web /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --to ./configs/
  komando download backups 2026/db.sql.gz
  komando download backups reports/ -r --to ./reports
  komando download web1 /var/backups/db.sql.gz --continue
  komando download web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --to - > nginx.conf

flags.usage: go on with a copy that was cut off: keep the part already at the destination when it matches the source, send the rest, then check the whole file (sha256)

flags.usage: replace files that already exist on this computer

commands.short: The environment variables komando reads
commands.long:
The environment variables komando reads.

  KOMANDO_HOME        where komando keeps its data (default ~/.komando)
  KOMANDO_OUTPUT      json or text when -o is not given
  KOMANDO_ACTOR       the name the audit log gives you

commands.short: Run a shell command on one or many servers in parallel
commands.long:
Runs COMMAND through the login shell on every server TARGET picks
(PowerShell on Windows servers). Each server's result has its stdout,
stderr, exit_code and duration. A non-zero exit on any server makes
komando exit 5. A refused connection or login exits 4; a server that does
not answer within --connect-timeout exits 7 (CONNECT_TIMEOUT).

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when the command matches a
destructive rule: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to
go on, and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; on a protected
server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

If the connection breaks while the command runs, that server's result has
error code CONNECTION_LOST (exit 4) and the output that came so far: the
command may still be running there, or may have finished. Check with a
read-only command before running it again. For long tasks over a shaky link
use `komando job start` and `komando job wait`: they survive a drop.

Commands that destroy things (rm -rf /, mkfs, reboot, DROP DATABASE, ...)
and any change on a production server: at a terminal komando asks you
first. --yes and --allow-dangerous answer that question in advance, for
scripts. --read-only says the command only looks: it runs only commands
komando knows only read (cat, grep, df, systemctl status ...) and refuses
any other, so a production server does not ask.

--script FILE runs a script from this computer instead: it is sent to the
interpreter (from its #! line, else sh; --interpreter to choose) as input,
so nothing is left on the server. --arg values become $1, $2 ... .
commands.example:
komando exec web1 -- uptime
  komando exec @web -P 20 -- 'df -h / | tail -1'
  komando exec tag:prod --sudo -- systemctl is-active nginx
  komando exec db1 --read-only -- df -h
  komando exec @web --script ./deploy.sh --arg v1.2.3 --sudo
  komando exec db1 --script ./backup.py --interpreter python3
  cat deploy.sh | komando exec web1 --stdin-file - -- 'bash -s'

commands.long:
What komando's exit codes mean.

  0 ok          1 error           2 usage           3 not found
  4 connect     5 failed on the server              6 blocked for safety

-o json shows the error code (USAGE, PROTECTED_TARGET ...) and a hint.

commands.short: Save servers, conns, VPNs, recipes and settings to a file
commands.long:
Saves your list to a file (komando-export/1, always JSON) that
`komando import komando FILE` reads on another computer. Passwords and key
files are never in it (only in a sealed file); it lists the secrets and keys
to bring along. With a
TARGET (@prod, kind:host, web1,web2) only those servers, conns and VPNs are
saved; without one also your recipes, deny rules and settings. Without --to
it prints the same JSON.

Safety: it only reads; with --sealed or --for-phone: only a person at a
terminal can run it; on a protected server or conn, a person's yes (--yes)
as well.

--sealed writes the same list with the passwords it uses into one sealed
file, for moving to another computer: komando asks for a passphrase twice
(15 or more characters), hidden, and the file opens only with it.
--for-phone seals the file to the iPhone app's key instead: komando asks
for the key file the phone shared and the key check the phone shows. Both
print a check phrase of six words; the phone shows the same words for the
file it got. --with-keys adds the private keys the servers use.

Only a person at a terminal can make a sealed file: an AI agent gets
NEEDS_PERSON, and a dry run says what would be sealed.
commands.example:
komando export --to komando-backup.json
  komando export @prod --to prod.json
  komando export kind:host --to servers.json
  komando import komando komando-backup.json      # on the other computer
  komando export --sealed --to move.kmdseal       # with passwords; asks a passphrase
  komando export --for-phone --to phone.kmdseal   # for the iPhone app; asks for its key

commands.short: System facts: OS and support, updates, Docker, open ports
commands.long:
Run this first on a server you do not know yet: it tells an agent which
package manager, init system and tools exist, so later commands fit the
server.

It also reports what needs attention: whether the OS still gets security
updates (Ubuntu ESM, Debian LTS, end of life), pending and security updates
(from the server's package index, which it does not refresh), a needed
reboot, passwordless sudo, Docker and the Swarm role, PM2 apps, listening
ports and services added by hand under /etc/systemd/system.

On Windows servers it reports the Windows version and its support dates,
pending updates from the Windows Update cache, a pending reboot, stopped
automatic services and listening ports.

--only load,mem,disks runs just those probes (load and CPUs; memory and
swap; every file system), in about a second, for an app that polls; the
other keys are left out. --only system gives the OS name and version and
the time the server has been up. On Windows the full probe runs and only
those keys are kept.

It only reads, and it uses sudo only when sudo works without a password.
A value komando cannot read is null ("unknown"), never 0 or false; read
data.results[].data.warnings first.
commands.example:
komando facts web1
  komando facts @prod -o json
  komando facts web1 --only load,mem,disks -o json
  komando facts web1 --only system

flags.name: only
flags.usage: run only these sections, comma-separated: disks, load, mem, system (fast, for polling; the other keys are left out)

commands.short: Files on servers: read, edit, undo an edit, move, remove
commands.long:
Reads and changes files on servers over SFTP and returns structured results.
Use --sudo for files that root owns: a read runs `sudo cat`, a write goes to
a temporary file first and then into place with `sudo install`.

For an agent, `fs replace` is the way to edit a config file: it fails unless
the old text matches exactly once (or --all), and --backup keeps a .bak
copy.
commands.example:
komando fs list web1 /etc/nginx
  komando fs cat web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
  komando fs replace web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --old 'worker_connections 512' --new 'worker_connections 1024' --backup --dry-run
  komando fs replace web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --old 'worker_connections 512' --new 'worker_connections 1024' --backup
  komando fs restore web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf     # undo the edit

commands.short: Edit a file on servers by replacing exact text
commands.long:
Replaces --old with --new in PATH. On a group (@web) every server gets the
same edit; each server's result says what changed there, and a server where
--old is not found fails on its own (NO_MATCH) while the others are changed.
Run it with --dry-run first to see each server's diff.

komando fs replace web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --old 'worker_connections 768;' --new 'worker_connections 4096;' --sudo --backup

  komando fs replace web1 /etc/ssh/sshd_config --regex --old '(?m)^#?PasswordAuthentication .*$' --new 'PasswordAuthentication no' --sudo

it is now is kept as a new backup first, so you can undo the restore too.

to see the change without making it.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or

  komando fs restore web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --copy /etc/nginx/nginx.conf.bak --sudo

commands.long:
Prints the rules an AI agent follows with komando. At a terminal it shows
the short rules; --all prints the whole playbook, and a TOPIC prints one
part. Piped (as an agent reads it), it prints the whole playbook as JSON.

commands.short: Add the komando skill to Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI
commands.long:
Teaches Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Gemini CLI to use komando safely.
Then restart the agent. In Codex, also approve the guard once in /hooks.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

It adds the komando skill (komando/SKILL.md) to the folders AI agents read
skills from: ~/.claude/skills (Claude Code) and ~/.agents/skills (Codex,
Cursor, Gemini CLI and others). The agent then uses komando by itself
whenever a task touches a server, database, cache or storage.

It also adds a guard: before the agent reads a file or runs a shell command
on this computer, komando checks it and stops the ones that would read
secrets (~/.komando, private keys, .env files, credential stores, all
environment variables at once) or use ssh around komando. It goes into
Claude Code (.claude/settings.json), and into Cursor (.cursor/hooks.json),
Gemini CLI (.gemini/settings.json, v0.26+) and Codex (.codex/hooks.json;
approve it once in /hooks) where their folders exist. Skip it with
--no-guard.

Safe to run again, for example after an update: a changed file is kept as
.bak. `komando guide uninstall` takes the skill and the guard out again.
commands.example:
komando guide install             # for every project on this computer
  komando guide install --project   # only for the folder you are in
  komando guide install --dry-run   # show where it would go

flags.name: no-guard
flags.usage: do not add the guard that keeps AI agents away from secret files on this computer

commands.short: Take the komando skill and guard out of your AI agents
commands.long:
Removes what `komando guide install` added: komando/SKILL.md in
~/.claude/skills and ~/.agents/skills, and komando's guard entries in
.claude/settings.json, .cursor/hooks.json, .gemini/settings.json and
.codex/hooks.json. Everything else in those files stays; a changed file is
kept as .bak. Taking the guard away from an AI agent lets it read secret
files on this computer again, so an agent needs a person's yes (--yes).

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when it removes komando's
guard from an AI agent's settings: it weakens a safety check: a person's yes
(--yes).
commands.example:
komando guide uninstall             # from your home folder
  komando guide uninstall --project   # from the folder you are in
  komando guide uninstall --dry-run   # show what it would remove

commands.short: Trust servers through the CA that signs their host keys
commands.long:
A host CA vouches for the host keys of the servers its patterns match, as an
@cert-authority line in known_hosts does. A server that shows a host
certificate from a trusted CA, for the name komando dials, is trusted
without a pin. Adding a CA trusts every server it ever signs, so only a
person at a terminal can add one. Removing one, and putting a key on the
never-trust list, anyone may do.
commands.example:
komando host ca add corp --key ~/corp-ca.pub --hosts '*.corp.example' --dry-run
  komando host ca list
  komando host ca rm corp
  komando host ca revoke --key old-ca.pub

commands.short: Trust a CA for the servers its patterns match (person only)
commands.long:
Trusts the CA in --key (a .pub file) for the host names in --hosts, or reads
the @cert-authority lines of a known_hosts file (--from); its @revoked lines
go on the never-trust list. A pattern names at least the domain
(*.corp.example, web*.corp.example, 10.1.2.*): '*' and '*.com' are refused.
--dry-run shows the patterns as they are kept and the servers they match
now. Only a person at a terminal can add a CA: it trusts every server it
ever signs.

Safety: only a person at a terminal can run it.
commands.example:
komando host ca add corp --key ~/corp-ca.pub --hosts '*.corp.example' --dry-run
  komando host ca add corp --from ~/.ssh/known_hosts

flags.name: from
flags.usage: a known_hosts file: read its @cert-authority and @revoked lines

flags.name: hosts
flags.usage: server name patterns the CA may vouch for (*.corp.example,10.1.2.*)

flags.name: key
flags.usage: the CA's public key file (.pub)

komando host ca list
  komando host ca list -o json   # what the apps read

commands.short: Never trust a host key or a CA key again
commands.long:
Puts the key in FILE.pub on the never-trust list (an @revoked line): no
server is reached with it as its host key, no certificate it signed or holds
is trusted, and it cannot be pinned or added as a CA.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.
commands.example:
komando host ca revoke --key old-ca.pub
  komando host ca revoke --key old-ca.pub --dry-run

flags.name: key
flags.usage: the public key file (.pub) never to trust

commands.short: Stop trusting a server CA
commands.long:
Stops trusting the CA: its servers are checked against their pins again.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.
commands.example:
komando host ca rm corp
  komando host ca rm corp --dry-run

commands.short: Change one or more servers (only the flags you pass change)
commands.long:
Changes only the settings you pass. Give one name, several names, or a
selector (@group, tag:prod, 'web-*') to change many servers at once. Try
--dry-run first to see which servers would change.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when --proxy-command matches
a destructive rule: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name
to go on, and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; with
--protected=false: it weakens a safety check: a person's yes (--yes); with
--proxy-command, when an AI agent runs it (the proxy command runs on this
computer): it weakens a safety check: a person's yes (--yes); on a protected
server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

--protected marks a production server: komando asks you before every change,
and an AI agent needs your yes in a window. Changing the login of a
production server, or turning its protection off, asks the same way; one yes
covers every server in the command.
commands.example:
komando host edit web1 --add-tag canary --label env=prod --sudo-ref secret:web1-sudo
  komando host edit web1 -g web -t prod          # -g/-t add a group/tag
  komando host edit db1 --protected              # production: ask before changes
  komando host edit @ubuntu --sudo-ref secret:ubuntu-sudo --dry-run
  komando host edit web1 web2 web3 --user deploy
  komando host edit vps1 --ask-password          # type a new password (hidden)
  komando host edit web2 --login ask             # never store its password; type it at every connect
  komando host edit web2 --login key --key deploy   # log in with a key komando names
  komando host edit bastion --forward-agent      # lend it your ssh-agent (asks first)

commands.short: List servers
commands.long: Same as `komando list kind:host`.
commands.example:
komando host list
  komando host list @web

flags.name: limit
flags.usage: show at most this many items (0 = all)

commands.short: Rename a server and every reference to it
commands.long:
Gives a server a new name. Everything about it stays: address, login,
references, protected mark, groups, tags and labels. Servers, conns and
tunnels that reach other things through it (--via), and its jobs and
tunnels, follow the new name. Pinned host keys belong to the address, so
they stay. Renaming a protected server needs --yes.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.
commands.example:
komando host rename web1 web-01
  komando host rename db1 prod-db1 --dry-run   # what would change
  komando host rename db1 prod-db1 --yes   # after a person's yes

commands.short: Remove servers (from komando only)
commands.long:
Remove servers from your list. The servers are not touched, and their pinned
host keys stay.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.
commands.example:
komando host rm web3
  komando host rm @old --dry-run     # what a selector would remove
  komando host rm 'tmp-*'

commands.short: Show all settings of a server (secrets as references, never values)
commands.example: komando host show web1

commands.short: Print the OpenSSH command komando would use for a server (person only)
commands.long:
Prints the ssh command that reaches the server with the same address, user,
key, known_hosts file and --via path komando uses. A server behind --via
servers gets a ProxyCommand per hop (ssh -W), so every hop uses its own key.
A SOCKS VPN becomes nc -X 5; VPNs that run inside komando cannot be used by
OpenSSH: use `komando shell SERVER` for those. A key made with komando key
gen is never written to a file: it goes to your running ssh-agent
(SSH_AUTH_SOCK) for one hour, and the line picks it by its public key.

Safety: only a person at a terminal can run it.
commands.example:
komando host ssh-command web1
  $(komando host ssh-command web1 -o text)      # open a shell with OpenSSH

commands.short: Check that servers answer and let you in
commands.long: Same as `komando test`.
commands.example:
komando host test web1
  komando host test @prod --wait 2m

flags.name: wait
flags.usage: test again every few seconds until every target passes, for up to this long (like 5m)

commands.short: Pin the SSH host keys of servers (--reset after a rebuild)
commands.long:
Fetches the server's host key and stores it in komando's known_hosts, like
ssh-keyscan plus ssh-keygen -R. The key is fetched the way komando reaches
the server: directly, or through its --via servers, VPN or proxy command.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when an AI agent pins a first
host key while host keys are strict: it weakens a safety check: a person's
yes (--yes); with --reset, when a key is pinned: only a person at a terminal
can run it; on a protected server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

A key that is already pinned is left as it is. If a different key is
pinned, the server may be an impostor (HOSTKEY_MISMATCH): check the new
fingerprint another way, then replace the pin with --reset. Only a person
at a terminal replaces a pin: komando shows the old and the new key and
asks once; an AI agent or a script gets NEEDS_PERSON, whatever flags it
adds. With --dry-run nothing is fetched or changed; it only counts the
pinned entries --reset would replace.

TARGET can be many servers (@group, tag:, 'web*', a,b): after a rebuild of a
whole group, --reset replaces all their keys after a single yes, which names
every server with its new key. Each server is in results, with its old and
new fingerprint; a server whose key changed is refused without --reset, the
others are pinned.

With --fingerprint SHA256:..., the key is pinned only when the server shows
that key: compare-then-pin in one step, for a fingerprint read from the
server's console or a cloud provider. Any other key stops with
HOSTKEY_MISMATCH and nothing is pinned. It takes one server, and the
fingerprint of the key type the server offers (key_type in the answer).
commands.example:
komando host trust web1
  komando host trust web1 --reset --dry-run   # how many pinned keys would go
  komando host trust web1 --reset             # after a real rebuild (a person, at a terminal)
  komando host trust @web                 # pin new servers; changed keys are refused
  komando host trust @web --reset         # after rebuilding the whole group: one yes
  komando host trust web1 --fingerprint SHA256:pVt2...  # pin only this key

flags.name: fingerprint
flags.usage: pin only if the server shows the key with this SHA256: fingerprint (one server)

flags.name: reset
flags.usage: replace the key pinned before (a person at a terminal only)

with --reset, when a key is pinned

commands.short: Bring in what you have: ssh config, .pgpass, my.cnf, .env
commands.long:
Adds servers, conns, VPNs and recipes from files you already have.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when an imported ProxyCommand
matches a destructive rule: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types
the name to go on, and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; when
an AI agent imports a server with a proxy command (it runs on this computer;
without --yes the server is left out): it weakens a safety check: a person's
yes (--yes); SOURCE kubeconfig, when an AI agent imports a context whose
login runs a program or sends a file of this computer: it weakens a safety
check: a person's yes (--yes); SOURCE komando, when the file is sealed
(export --sealed): a person types its passphrase: only a person at a
terminal can run it.

Sources:
  ssh-config  servers from your OpenSSH config (default ~/.ssh/config)
  pgpass      PostgreSQL databases and their passwords (default ~/.pgpass)
  mycnf       MySQL/MariaDB databases from [client] sections (default ~/.my.cnf)
  env         database, cache and storage URLs (DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, ...) (default .env)
  kubeconfig  Kubernetes clusters, one conn per context (default ~/.kube/config)
  docker      container registries you are logged in to (default ~/.docker/config.json)
  filezilla   SFTP sites from FileZilla's Site Manager (default ~/.config/filezilla/sitemanager.xml)
  rclone      SFTP remotes from rclone (default ~/.config/rclone/rclone.conf)
  putty       SSH sessions from PuTTY (a .reg file: `reg export HKCU\Software\SimonTatham\PuTTY\Sessions putty.reg`)
  mobaxterm   SSH sessions from MobaXterm (a .mxtsessions file: right-click User sessions, Export all sessions to file)
  securecrt   SSH2 sessions from SecureCRT (File > Export Settings gives an .xml file; or its Sessions folder)
  aws         an S3 storage conn per bucket of each AWS profile (uses the profile; no key is copied) (default ~/.aws/config)
  aws-ec2     a server per running EC2 instance of each AWS profile, in its region (read only, with the profile's login) (default ~/.aws/config)
  dbeaver     databases from DBeaver (passwords set afterwards) (default ~/Library/DBeaverData/workspace6/General/.dbeaver/data-sources.json)
  komando     a file made by `komando export` (moving to another computer)
  csv         servers from a spreadsheet (CSV, first row names the columns: name, address (or ip), user, port, key, identity, password-ref, sudo-ref, via, groups (or role), tags, protected, notes)

Passwords go to the vault (as <name>-pass; a kubeconfig as
<name>-kubeconfig) and are referenced from the conn; they are never
printed. Existing names are skipped unless
--overwrite (replacing a protected one also needs --yes). Proxy commands
from an ssh config run on this computer, so an AI agent needs a person's yes
for them. Try --dry-run first to see what would be added.
commands.example:
komando import ssh-config --dry-run
  komando import pgpass
  komando import env ./app/.env --group shop
  komando import komando backup.json

SOURCE komando, when the file is sealed (export --sealed): a person types its passphrase

commands.short: Long-running jobs on servers: start, follow, wait for, stop
commands.long:
A long command should not hold up an agent's tool call. `job start` starts
the command in the background on each server and returns the job IDs at
once; it keeps running when the connection drops. Check on it with `job
status` or `job logs --offset N` (pass back next_offset), or wait with `job
wait --timeout`.
commands.example:
komando job start @web -- ./deploy.sh
  komando job list
  komando job wait j1103-101500-ab12cd34 --timeout 30m
  komando job logs j1103-101500-ab12cd34 --limit 50

commands.short: Stop a job: send a signal to its process group (default TERM)
commands.long:
Send a signal to a job's process group (default TERM). A job that already
ended is left as it is.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.
commands.example:
komando job kill j1103-101500-ab12cd34
  komando job kill j1103-101500-ab12cd34 --dry-run
  komando job kill j1103-101500-ab12cd34 --signal KILL

flags.usage: signal name or number (TERM, KILL, INT, HUP ...)

flags.name: sudo
flags.usage: send the signal with sudo (for jobs started with --sudo)

commands.short: List the jobs komando started (--refresh asks the servers)
commands.example:
komando job list
  komando job list --refresh --target web1

flags.name: limit
flags.usage: show at most this many jobs, newest first (0 = all)

flags.name: refresh
flags.usage: ask each server for the job's current state

flags.name: target
flags.usage: only jobs on these servers (a selector, like @web)

commands.short: Read a job's output, piece by piece or its last lines
commands.long:
Read a job's output piece by piece (--offset with the next_offset of the
last call), or its last --limit N lines.
commands.example:
komando job logs j1103-101500-ab12cd34 --limit 100
  komando job logs j1103-101500-ab12cd34 --offset 4096   # only what is new since then

flags.usage: return only the last N lines instead (0 = read from --offset)

flags.name: max-bytes

commands.long:
Forget jobs and delete their log folders on the server (a running job needs
`job kill` or --kill).

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.
commands.example:
komando job rm j1103-101500-ab12cd34
  komando job rm j1103-101500-ab12cd34 --dry-run

flags.usage: keep the job's log folder on the server

flags.name: kill

commands.short: Start a background job on each server TARGET picks
commands.long:
Starts COMMAND in the background on each server TARGET picks and returns
the job IDs at once; the job keeps running when the connection drops.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when the command matches a
destructive rule: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to
go on, and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; on a protected
server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

--script FILE runs a script from this computer as the job, like
`exec --script`: it goes to the interpreter (from its #! line, else sh;
--interpreter to choose) and its copy on the server is removed as soon as
the job has opened it. --arg values become $1, $2 ... .

--stdin-file FILE is the command's input ('-' for komando's own stdin), as
in exec. --sudo-user USER runs it as USER with sudo -u. --timeout stops the
job after that long (as job kill does; job status then says it timed out);
without it a job has no time limit.
commands.example:
komando job start db1 -- 'pg_dump app | gzip > /backup/app.sql.gz'
  komando job start @web --sudo -- 'apt-get update && apt-get -y upgrade'
  komando job start @web --script ./deploy.sh --arg v1.2.3 --sudo
  komando job start db1 --sudo-user postgres --stdin-file ./migrate.sql --timeout 2h -- 'psql app'

commands.short: Wait until the jobs end
commands.long:
Waits until the job ends, checking every --interval. --timeout (default 10m)
is how long to wait; the job keeps running after it (exit 7, WAIT_TIMEOUT).

A dropped connection does not stop the wait: komando connects again and
keeps waiting. Give several job IDs (the ones `job start` printed for a
group of servers) to wait for all of them at once.
commands.example:
komando job wait j1103-101500-ab12cd34 --timeout 30m
  komando job wait j1103-101500-ab12cd34 j1103-101500-ef56ab78

flags.usage: how often to check

commands.short: SSH keys: make, add, put on servers, take off
commands.example:
komando key gen deploy
  komando key deploy deploy @web --dry-run
  komando key deploy deploy @web
  komando key list

commands.short: Add a private key file you already have (komando keeps its path)
commands.long:
Adds a private key file you already have to komando's key list; the file
stays where it is. For a key with a passphrase, store the passphrase in the
vault and pass --passphrase-ref secret:NAME.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

An OpenSSH user certificate next to the key (FILE-cert.pub) is used at
login, as ssh does; --cert names one kept somewhere else.
commands.example:
komando key add personal ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
  komando key add personal ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 --dry-run
  komando key add corp ~/.ssh/id_corp --cert ~/.ssh/corp-ca/id_corp-cert.pub
  komando secret set id-pass && komando key add work ~/.ssh/id_work --passphrase-ref secret:id-pass

flags.name: cert
flags.usage: an OpenSSH user certificate for the key (default: FILE-cert.pub next to it, if there)

flags.name: passphrase-ref
flags.usage: passphrase reference for encrypted keys (secret:NAME | env:VAR | ...)

commands.short: Install a public key in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (like ssh-copy-id)
commands.long:
Installs a public key on servers, like ssh-copy-id. KEY is a key in
komando's key list or a .pub file. komando logs in the way each server is
set up now (a password, for example) and appends the key to
~/.ssh/authorized_keys unless it is already there. With --set-default the
servers then log in with this key.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.
commands.example:
komando key gen deploy && komando key deploy deploy @web --set-default
  komando key deploy ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub web1
  komando key deploy ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub web1 --dry-run

flags.name: set-default
flags.usage: servers that got the key log in with it from now on

commands.short: Change a key's passphrase reference or certificate
commands.long:
Sets where komando finds the passphrase of an encrypted key. Store the
passphrase with `komando secret set NAME` first and pass secret:NAME;
--unset passphrase-ref clears it.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

--cert FILE gives the key an OpenSSH user certificate (for a key komando
made, or one kept away from the key file); --unset cert goes back to
FILE-cert.pub next to the key.
commands.example:
komando secret set work-key-pass
  komando key edit work --passphrase-ref secret:work-key-pass
  komando key edit work --passphrase-ref secret:work-key-pass --dry-run
  komando key edit work --unset passphrase-ref
  komando key edit deploy --cert ~/Downloads/deploy-cert.pub

flags.usage: an OpenSSH user certificate for the key

flags.name: passphrase-ref

it runs out; then their commands stop with AWS_LOGIN_REQUIRED and the same
command renews it. Logging in is for a person: an AI agent gets
NEEDS_PERSON and asks you to run it. A profile with keys in
~/.aws/credentials needs no login.

komando login aws --profile prod       # opens the browser; confirm the code shown
  komando login aws                      # the profile in AWS_PROFILE, else default
  komando login aws --profile prod --dry-run   # which sign-in page, without logging in

commands.short: Upgrade all or the given packages (--dry-run lists them)

Without --security: upgrades every package, or the given ones (--dry-run
lists what would change).

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; with --security, when an
update would remove a package the server needs: dangerous, it cannot be
undone: a person types the name to go on, and an AI agent or a script needs
--allow-dangerous; on a protected server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as
well.

--security installs only the security updates, one server at a time. On
apt servers komando uses unattended-upgrade when it is installed (it picks
security origins only and follows the server's own settings), otherwise
apt-get --only-upgrade of the listed packages, keeping changed config
files. On dnf/yum it runs "upgrade --security", on zypper "patch
--category security". needrestart is kept from
restarting services during the run; the result lists the services that
need it.

After each server komando compares the state with the one before. When
fewer containers run or a unit has failed, it stops and leaves the other
servers as they are (--keep-going patches them anyway). It never reboots:
reboot_required says when a server needs one, use `komando reboot`.

The upgrade runs detached on the server, so a dropped connection does not
break it. It waits up to 30 minutes per server (--timeout changes it).
Where komando cannot pick the security updates (apk, pacman, dnf/yum
repositories without security notices) the server stops with
SECURITY_UNSUPPORTED: use `komando pkg upgrade` without --security there.
commands.example:
komando pkg upgrade web1 --dry-run   # see what would change first
  komando pkg upgrade web1 openssl
  komando pkg upgrade @web --security --dry-run
  komando pkg upgrade @web --security

on again everywhere; --rm-server and --rm-group switch it on again on those

commands.long:
Read and send messages on Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS, SQS and Pub/Sub. Add a
queue with `komando queue add`.

info, ls, describe, peek, groups and lag only read: peek reads Kafka
messages without joining a consumer group, gives RabbitMQ and Pub/Sub
messages straight back, reads NATS stream messages by their number, and
receives SQS messages without hiding or deleting them, so nothing is
removed. send and create change (production queues ask first); rm and purge
delete messages, so they also need --allow-dangerous. Try any change with
--dry-run first. In RabbitMQ words a topic is a queue; in NATS words it is
a stream. Pub/Sub keeps messages in subscriptions: peek and purge take a
subscription, and groups lists them.
commands.example:
komando queue add prod-kafka kafka://10.0.0.8:9092 --via web1
  komando queue list prod-kafka
  komando queue peek prod-kafka orders -n 5
  komando queue send prod-kafka orders --value '{"id": 42}' --dry-run
  komando queue lag prod-kafka billing

commands.short: Read the newest (or oldest) messages without removing any
commands.long:
Kafka: read messages straight from the topic's partitions. No consumer
group is joined and no offset is committed, so no application notices and
nothing is removed. By default the newest -n messages over all partitions;
--oldest reads the first ones still kept.

RabbitMQ: take the first -n messages of the queue (the next ones a consumer
would get) and give them all back. Nothing is removed, but RabbitMQ marks
them redelivered, and a quorum queue counts each peek as a delivery: peek
stops (DELIVERY_LIMIT_NEAR) before a message runs out of them.

NATS: read messages straight from the stream by their sequence number. No
consumer is made and nothing is acknowledged, so nothing is removed, also
from a work-queue stream. The newest -n by default, --oldest for the first.

Amazon SQS: receive messages with a visibility timeout of 0 and never
delete them, so they stay and consumers can receive them at once. SQS gives
messages in no set order, so this is a sample of what waits. Every receive
counts toward a dead-letter queue's maxReceiveCount: peek stops
(DELIVERY_LIMIT_NEAR) before a message runs out of receives.

Google Cloud Pub/Sub: TOPIC is a subscription (messages wait there, not
in a topic). peek pulls messages without acknowledging them and gives them
straight back (ack deadline 0), so they stay and are delivered again at
once. With a dead-letter topic each pull counts as a delivery: peek stops
(DELIVERY_LIMIT_NEAR) before a message runs out of them.

Values that are not UTF-8 text are shown as base64.
commands.example:
komando queue peek prod-kafka orders
  komando queue peek prod-kafka orders -n 50 --partition 2
  komando queue peek prod-kafka orders --oldest -n 5

commands.short: Publish one message
commands.long:
Publish one message to an existing topic (or queue) and wait until the
server keeps it. The value comes from --value, from a file (--from FILE;
'-' is stdin), or from data piped on stdin. --dry-run checks the topic and
the partition and sends nothing.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

Kafka: --key picks the partition the usual way (the same key always goes
to the same partition); --partition picks one itself.
RabbitMQ: the message goes straight to the queue (the default exchange),
persistent, with --header values as its headers.
NATS: TOPIC is a subject that a stream keeps (orders.new); komando checks
which stream, publishes, and waits for the stream's acknowledgement.
Amazon SQS: text only; --header values become message attributes. A FIFO
queue (name.fifo) needs --key, the message group.
Google Cloud Pub/Sub: TOPIC is a topic; --header values become message
attributes and --key is the ordering key.
commands.example:
komando queue send prod-kafka orders --value '{"id": 42, "status": "paid"}' --key 42
  komando queue send prod-kafka orders --from ./order.json --header source=support
  komando queue send prod-kafka orders --value test --dry-run

commands.short: Reboot servers one at a time and check each came back
commands.long:
Reboots each server in turn: komando asks it to reboot, waits until SSH
answers again, and checks that it started anew (a new boot id). The next
server is rebooted only when the one before came back; a server that does
not come back within --wait stops the rest.

Safety: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to go on,
and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; on a protected server
or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

A reboot is a destructive action: it needs --allow-dangerous (and --yes or
the approval for protected servers). Try --dry-run first.
commands.example:
komando reboot web1 --dry-run
  komando reboot @web --wait 10m --dry-run
  komando reboot @web --allow-dangerous --wait 10m   # after a person's yes

`komando registry add ghcr registry://myuser@ghcr.io --ask-password`,
or bring in the ones you use with `komando import docker`.

commands.short: Rename one entry, or all names starting with OLD (--starts-with)
commands.long:
Without --starts-with: renames the one server, conn, VPN, secret, key or
group named OLD, as `komando host rename` and the others do. When OLD names
two kinds of entry (a server and a secret), it says which commands to use.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

With --starts-with: renames every server, conn, VPN, secret, key and group
whose name starts with OLD: OLD is replaced with NEW. When OLD ends in -,
the name OLD without it is renamed too (--starts-with shop- acme-shop- turns
group shop into acme-shop).

Every reference follows, as with `host rename` and `secret rename`: --via
paths, password, sudo, key, preshared key and passphrase references,
secret:NAME options in conn URLs, the key a server uses, group membership,
jobs and tunnels. A key komando made (key gen) lives in the sealed store, so
no file moves; a key file you added stays where it is. The protected mark,
labels, notes and creation time stay. Names inside URLs (a bucket, a
database user) are the resource's own and do not change.

--in-notes also replaces old names in notes, and --in-labels in label
values: server, conn, VPN and secret names as whole words, a group written
@NAME, and a pattern such as shop-db-* when it matches the same entries
after the rename. OLD without its -, group names without @, key names, and a
name that is also the user, host, bucket or database in a conn URL stay:
they often mean something else. The result lists each one it keeps ("kept"),
and each label value that names an old entry, with or without --in-labels.

Everything changes in one step, or nothing does: a new name that is taken
(or two old names that would get one new name) stops it before anything
is written. When NEW starts with OLD, names that start with NEW already
are left alone, so a second run changes nothing.

Renaming protected servers and conns needs --yes once, for all of them (an
AI agent's --yes opens one window for a person). See what would change with
--dry-run first. --kind renames only some kinds; references still follow. To
rename one entry, use host rename, conn rename, vpn rename, secret rename,
key rename or group rename.
commands.example:
komando rename web1 web-01 --dry-run                 # one entry, whatever kind it is
  komando rename --starts-with shop- acme-shop- --dry-run   # the old -> new list and every reference
  komando rename --starts-with shop- acme-shop- --yes   # after a person's yes
  komando rename --starts-with old-registry registry --kind conn,secret
  komando rename --starts-with lab- test- --in-notes --in-labels --dry-run

commands.short: How komando keeps a change from going wrong
commands.long:
How komando keeps a change from going wrong.

  --dry-run           every change can show what it would do first
  protected targets   a change asks [y/N] at your terminal; scripts and agents need --yes
  dangerous commands  rm -rf /, DROP DATABASE ...: you type the name; scripts need --allow-dangerous
  read only           db query, cache run and cluster run only read unless you add --write
  audit               komando audit shows every change and who asked for it

An AI agent is never asked: it gets exit 6 and a person allows the flag in a
window on the screen. See docs/features/safety.md.

commands.short: Every command, flag and exit code, machine-readable
commands.long: Machine-readable reference of every command, flag, exit code and selector.
commands.example:
komando schema            # everything
  komando schema exec        # one command subtree
  komando schema host.add    # one command, as named in the envelope
  komando schema --compact   # paths + short descriptions only

flags.name: compact
flags.usage: only paths and short descriptions

commands.short: Saved passwords and tokens: store, check, use as secret:NAME
commands.long:
Save a password once, then point to it as secret:NAME instead of typing it:
  komando secret set web1-pass
  komando host edit web1 --password-ref secret:web1-pass

komando shows a saved value only to a person: at a terminal with
`secret show --reveal`, or after "Allow once" in komando's window; never
to an AI agent. `secret check` compares a value with the saved one
without showing either. `secret rename` and `secret cp` rename and copy.

How it is stored: each secret sealed with AES-256-GCM in
~/.komando/store.db. The random key is in the OS keychain (or in store.key
where there is none, or with KOMANDO_KEYCHAIN=off), or comes from
$KOMANDO_VAULT_PASS when that is set at first use (`secret passphrase`
changes it).

A --password-ref (and the other -ref flags) can also read a password your
team keeps elsewhere; komando reads it when needed and never stores it:
  env:VAR  file:PATH  vault:PATH#FIELD  aws-sm:NAME[#KEY]  gcp-sm:NAME[@PROJECT]
  azure-kv:VAULT/NAME[#KEY]  op://VAULT/ITEM/FIELD  bw://ITEM/FIELD  kdbx:FILE#GROUP/ENTRY
commands.example:
komando secret set prod-db-pass                   # typed hidden
  komando secret list
  komando conn edit prod-db --password-ref secret:prod-db-pass
  komando secret rm old-pass --dry-run

commands.short: Compare a typed value to a secret without showing either (person only)
commands.long:
Asks for a value (hidden, or from --from-env VAR or a pipe) and says whether
it is the stored one. When it is not, it says how they differ (only spaces
at the ends, only upper and lower case, or the number of characters), but
never shows either value.

Safety: only a person at a terminal can run it.

Only a person can run it: for an AI agent, a yes/no answer about a value it
picks would be a way to guess the secret one try at a time.
commands.example:
komando secret check vpn-pass            # type or paste it after the prompt
  pbpaste | komando secret check vpn-pass

flags.usage: read the value to compare from this environment variable

commands.long:
Stores the value of OLD under NEW as well. The value stays inside the vault:
it is never printed, so an AI agent can do this too. Nothing that uses OLD
changes.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

When NEW exists already, --overwrite replaces its value; when a protected
server or conn uses NEW, that also needs --yes.
commands.example:
komando secret cp db-pass db-pass-old
  komando secret cp db-pass db-pass-old --dry-run
  komando secret cp web-pass shared-pass --overwrite

commands.short: Keep the vault key in the OS keychain instead of store.key
commands.long:
Moves the vault's key out of the store.key file into the operating system's
keychain, so a copy of ~/.komando (a backup, a synced folder) no longer
opens the vault or its secrets. The vault gets a new key as it moves, so a
copy of store.key made before opens nothing either, and the vault keeps
every secret. --off moves the key back into store.key, which needs --yes.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when it turns the keychain
off: it weakens a safety check: a person's yes (--yes); without --off
(moving the key into the keychain): only a person at a terminal can run it.

Only a person at a terminal moves the key in: the keychain may ask them to
unlock it, and an AI agent or a script cannot answer that.
commands.example:
komando secret keychain
  komando secret keychain --dry-run
  komando secret keychain --off --dry-run
  komando secret keychain --off --yes   # after a person's yes

flags.usage: move the key back into store.key (needs --yes)

without --off (moving the key into the keychain)

commands.example: komando secret list

commands.short: Change the vault passphrase and encrypt the secrets again (person only)
commands.long:
Re-encrypts every secret in the vault under a new passphrase, so you can
change KOMANDO_VAULT_PASS without losing your secrets. A vault whose key is
in store.key or in the OS keychain gets a passphrase this way, and the old
key is removed once the new vault is saved and read back.

Safety: only a person at a terminal can run it.

The vault is opened the usual way: with KOMANDO_VAULT_PASS, store.key or the
keychain. When KOMANDO_VAULT_PASS does not open a passphrase vault (you
changed it already, say), komando asks for the current passphrase. Then it
asks for the new one twice, hidden; it needs 15 or more characters. Every
secret is decrypted before anything is written: if one cannot be, nothing
changes.

Afterwards, put the new passphrase in KOMANDO_VAULT_PASS wherever you set it
(your shell profile, a password manager, a launch agent), and restart any
background tunnel or VPN session komando runs: they still hold the old key.

--off goes back to a new random key in store.key (needs --yes): a copy of
~/.komando then opens the vault again. `komando secret keychain` can move
that key into the OS keychain.

Only a person at a terminal can run it: an AI agent that chose the
passphrase, or put the key back in store.key, could open the vault on its
own. Anyone can preview it with --dry-run.
commands.example:
komando secret passphrase               # asks for the new passphrase twice, hidden
  komando secret passphrase --dry-run
  komando secret passphrase --off --dry-run
  komando secret passphrase --off --yes   # after a person's yes

commands.long:
Renames OLD to NEW inside the vault, and points every server, conn, key and
VPN that used secret:OLD at secret:NEW in the same step, so nothing stops
working and nobody types the value again. The value is never printed, so an
AI agent can do this too. Scripts or notes of your own that name secret:OLD
are not changed.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

When NEW exists already, --overwrite replaces its value; when a protected
server or conn uses NEW, that also needs --yes.
commands.example:
komando secret rename vpn-password office-vpn-pass --dry-run
  komando secret rename vpn-password office-vpn-pass

flags.usage: replace NEW when it exists (what uses NEW then gets the value of OLD)

commands.short: Delete secrets for good
commands.long:
Delete secrets for good.

Safety: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to go on,
and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous.

komando secret rm old-pass
  komando secret rm a-pass b-pass --dry-run

commands.short: Run a local command with vault secrets in its environment
commands.long:
Starts COMMAND on this computer with the --env values in its environment. A
value secret:NAME is read from the vault right before the program starts, so
it is never in the command line or the shell history. The program starts
directly, without a shell, with your environment minus komando's own
KOMANDO_* variables and the values that unlock the vault. For an AI agent
with secrets, --env may add variables but never replace one komando sets
(HOME, PATH, USER, LANG, ...), and may not set what decides which code or
settings the program loads: LD_PRELOAD, DYLD_*, NODE_OPTIONS, PYTHON*,
BASH_ENV, a pager, an editor, an askpass helper, an rc file, a proxy, GIT_*,
SSH_*, XDG_*, a tool's config file (KUBECONFIG, DOCKER_CONFIG,
*_CONFIG_FILE, AWS_*_FILE, NPM_CONFIG_*) or a toolchain's (CC, CXX, GOFLAGS,
GOTOOLCHAIN, CARGO_*, RUSTC_WRAPPER, JAVA_HOME, MAVEN_OPTS). The program
gets HOME, USER and LOGNAME from your OS account (USERPROFILE on Windows),
LANG, LC_*, TERM, TMPDIR, TZ, the Windows system folders, a system PATH and
its --env values.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

The program's output goes through komando's masking: a vault value it
prints shows as [secret:NAME]. komando exits with the program's exit code.

For an AI agent every secret:NAME needs a person's yes (--yes, then
komando's window names the secrets and the program), since the program
could print a value in a form masking does not know. A secret a protected
server, conn or VPN uses asks a person at a terminal too.
commands.example:
komando secret run --env PGPASSWORD=secret:db-main -- psql -h 10.0.0.5 -U app
  komando secret run -e AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=secret:aws-ci -e AWS_REGION=eu-west-1 -- terraform plan
  komando secret run --dry-run --env TOKEN=secret:gh-token -- ./deploy.sh

flags.name: env
flags.usage: put KEY=VALUE or KEY=secret:NAME in the program's environment (repeatable)

commands.kind_note: decided by the program it starts on this computer

commands.short: Store a secret, typed hidden or from a variable or a pipe
commands.long:
Saves or replaces a password. Replacing one that a production server or
database uses asks first: it changes how komando logs in there. With --new
it only saves a new one: when NAME is in the vault already it stops with
SECRET_EXISTS and leaves the stored value alone.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

A value from a pipe loses the line breaks at its end (echo and pbpaste add
one). Spaces are kept, since a password can hold them; komando warns when
the value starts or ends with one, so a stray space copied with a password
is noticed. At the terminal, paste or type the value after the prompt
appears.
commands.example:
komando secret set web1-pass          # type or paste it after the prompt, nothing is shown
  komando secret set web1-pass --dry-run
  komando secret set db-pass --from-env DB_PASS
  pbpaste | komando secret set vpn-pass
  komando secret set api-token --new --from-env TOKEN   # never replaces one

flags.name: from-env
flags.usage: read the value from this environment variable

flags.name: new
flags.usage: only store a secret that is not in the vault yet; a taken NAME stops with SECRET_EXISTS

commands.short: Show that a secret exists, its value hidden
commands.long:
Says whether the secret exists and what uses it, without its value. A person
at a terminal can add --reveal to print it; from a program without a
terminal (the Komando Mac app), komando first asks the person in its own
window. AI agents never get the value (they reference it as secret:NAME
instead). A warning says when the value starts or ends with a space, tab or
line break, a common cause of a failing login; 'komando secret check NAME'
lets a person compare it.
commands.example:
komando secret show db-pass
  komando secret show db-pass --reveal | pbcopy   # a person, at a terminal

commands.short: Open a login shell on one server (person only)
commands.long:
Open a login shell on one server.

Safety: only a person at a terminal can run it.
commands.example: komando shell web1
commands.kind_note: an shellNote shell for a person: whatever they type

commands.short: Let an SSH key run komando here and nothing else (person only)
commands.long:
ssh-gate lets an SSH key (a phone's, say) run komando on this computer, and
nothing else: no shell, no file copy, no port forwarding. Add the key to
~/.ssh/authorized_keys with the line `komando ssh-gate line` prints; sshd
then runs ssh-gate for it, whatever the key asks for.

Safety: only a person at a terminal can run it.

ssh-gate takes the command the key sent (SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND) only when it
is one komando command. It splits it into words like a shell, but expands
nothing and runs no shell: ; | & > < $ and backquotes are refused unless
they are quoted. One KOMANDO_AGENT=NAME may come before komando.

komando then runs as for an AI agent: secret values stay [hidden], --reveal
and --allow-dangerous are refused, and --yes for a protected server needs a
person on this computer. Commands that need a person at a terminal (shell,
db shell, secret passphrase ...) are refused (a --shell-access key may open
`komando shell SERVER`: see ssh-gate line; that shell is full control of the
server, outside these rules). The key runs commands on servers, never one
that writes on this computer or reads a file here (a script, SQL or upload
source by path; '-' for the key's own input works): no download or cp to a
file here (download --to - and cp SRC - stream to the key's own output), no
change to servers, VPNs, settings, rules, secrets, keys or recipes in
komando, no update, no change on a sqlite file or a target at localhost or
127.x. With --read-only only commands that read run (db query and cache run
without --write), and only those that stay on the servers and conns in your
list: no net, no cert check of a website, no exec, job start, docker exec,
cluster exec or recipe run, unless the line also has --network. `komando
ssh-gate status` tells a key which it is. Every command a key runs or is
refused is in `komando audit`, with --name, even when the audit setting is
off.
commands.example:
komando ssh-gate line --name phone ~/phone.pub
  komando ssh-gate line --name phone-read --read-only 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA... phone'
commands.kind_note: runs the komando command an SSH key sent, when ssh-gate allows it

commands.short: Print the authorized_keys line that limits a key to komando
commands.long:
Prints the line to add to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on this computer, so the
key runs komando through ssh-gate and nothing else. PUBLIC_KEY is the key's
line (ssh-ed25519 AAAA... comment) or a .pub file holding it. The line names
this komando by its full path, as sshd does not search PATH.

A --read-only key runs only commands that read, and only those that stay
on the servers and conns in your list: no net checks, no cert check of
a website, and no exec, job start, docker exec, cluster exec or recipe run,
whose programs can connect anywhere and carry what they read in a URL or a
DNS name. Add --network too for a read key that may do those.

With --shell-access (not with --read-only) the key may also open a login
shell on one server: ssh -t HOST komando shell SERVER, word for word. Its
line has restrict,pty, so sshd gives it a terminal when it asks for one.
The shell is refused on a protected server, a Windows server or this
computer, with any other word or flag, without the terminal, and on every
server while you have deny rules of your own (komando policy list); db
shell and cluster shell stay refused. On the servers it opens on, the
shell is full control of the server, as the account komando logs in with:
what is typed is outside komando's per-command rules, masking and audit.
Give such a key only to a device you would give that login to. Each
session's start and end are in komando audit (key, server, how long, why
it ended), and a session with no input and no output for 30 minutes ends.
commands.example:
komando ssh-gate line --name phone ~/phone.pub
  komando ssh-gate line --name phone-read --read-only 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA... phone'
  komando ssh-gate line --name phone-checks --read-only --network ~/phone.pub
  komando ssh-gate line --name ops --shell-access ~/ops.pub
